h1: Green Bullet hops for raisin and spice in the bittering
title: Green Bullet Hops for Bittering | Craft Beer School
desc: Green Bullet hops from New Zealand: alpha range, the raisin and spice character in the kettle, dosing maths for a 1,000 litre batch and storage.
teaser: Green Bullet is a bittering hop with a character of its own. That character shows in dark and amber beers more than in pale ones.
standfirst: Green Bullet is a New Zealand hop grown mainly for its alpha acid. Used at 60 minutes it also leaves a spicy, resinous note with a hint of dried fruit. Here is how to dose it and where it fits.
sections:
Green Bullet comes from New Zealand and is grown for bittering. Alpha acid is high, typically quoted at 11 to 14% depending on crop. Brewers describe the character as spicy and resinous with a raisin-like depth when it is used for bittering. Most brewers keep it in the kettle at 60 minutes and use other hops for aroma.

Treat all numbers as the supplier's figures for that crop. Always use the alpha acid printed on your packet, not a book value. Our guide on bittering hops for clean lager bitterness compares the neutral choices that Green Bullet is an alternative to.

The working rule is milligrams of alpha acid per litre multiplied by utilisation. At 60 minutes in a wort of normal gravity, utilisation in a vigorous boil is often near 25%, but your kettle, boil intensity and wort gravity change it. Use your own figures from measured IBU if you have them.

As an illustration: for 30 IBU, you need about 120 mg per litre of alpha acid in the kettle (30 divided by 0.25). In 1,000 litres that is 120 g of alpha acid. With Green Bullet at 12.5% alpha, divide by 0.125 and you get about 960 g of pellets. Adjust for the actual alpha on the packet and your measured utilisation. Expect some loss to trub as well.
The raisin and spice in the glass

The bittering character shows most in beers that give it something to sit against. Malt sweetness and roast hold the dried fruit note. Amber ales, brown ales, porters and darker IPAs are natural fits. In a pale lager or a delicate wheat beer the resin and spice can read as coarse.

Compare it with its neighbours in a blind tasting before you decide. Our guide on Warrior hops covers a cleaner high alpha choice. Liberty covers a gentler spice.
Where it fits in a recipe

• Amber and brown ales: bitter with Green Bullet and add a soft finishing hop at flameout.
  • Dark IPAs and black IPAs: the resin supports roast without clashing.
  • Strong ales: a high alpha hop keeps the kettle volume of hops low when the beer is big.
  • Spiced or Belgian-style beers: the spice note can match added spice.

For pale ales and IPAs built around fruit, bitter with a neutral hop and keep Green Bullet out of the way. Read the related guide on Ekuanot for an example of a hop whose savoury side needs control.
Check alpha loss before you weigh

This is the floor detail. High alpha pellets lose alpha acid in storage, faster when warm. A packet bought at 12.5% alpha and stored for a year at room temperature can read well below that. If your packet carries a hop storage index, read it. Otherwise assume loss and verify with a measured IBU on the first batch. Weigh the pellets to the gram on a calibrated scale and record the lot number so you can trace any change in bitterness to a batch of hops.

Green Bullet reaches Indian brewers through importers, with delays and heat in transit. Ask your supplier for the harvest year and how the hops travelled. Keep pellets in sealed foil in a freezer, away from the brewhouse. If your supplier cannot get it, Magnum, Warrior or Columbus will do a similar bittering job with a cleaner profile. Run the dosing maths again with the new alpha, then taste the result side by side.

Do not expect to replace it one for one. Resin, spice and dried fruit are part of the reason to choose it in the first place. If a brewery wants the same raisin depth from a neutral hop, the honest answer is to add a little dark crystal malt to the grist and taste again.

Brew your usual amber ale twice, once bittered with Green Bullet and once with a neutral hop, both calculated to the same IBU. Keep everything else the same. Taste both after conditioning. If the Green Bullet beer shows raisin and spice without harshness, you have found a use. If it reads rough, move it to a stronger, darker beer or stop using it.
faqs: What does Green Bullet taste like?
Spicy and resinous with a raisin-like depth when used for bittering. Larger late additions can add green and grassy notes.
What alpha acid does Green Bullet have?
Typically quoted at 11 to 14%, depending on the crop. Always use the figure printed on your packet.
What can I use instead of Green Bullet?
Magnum, Warrior or Columbus bitter cleanly. Recalculate the dose from the new alpha acid and taste side by side.
Is Green Bullet good for pale lagers?
Usually not. The resin and spice read as coarse in a delicate beer. Amber, brown and darker beers suit it better.
